items.title: Today I will… review GitHub PRs
items.lede: Today I will show you how we can tackle one of the most common tasks when working in a development team or managing an open-source project, and that is working with Pull Requests. While we’re going to be using the GitHub tooling within Visual Studio for this, the approach would be very similar with Azure […]
items.text:
Today I will show you how we can tackle one of the most common tasks when working in a development team or managing an open-source project, and that is working with Pull Requests.

While we’re going to be using the GitHub tooling within Visual Studio for this, the approach would be very similar with Azure DevOps.

Getting our PRs

Start by opening the pull requests for your repository. Select Git → GitHub → View Pull Requests. You can also search for the command in the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P.

From here, Visual Studio will load all the PRs in the repo and group them to the ones that are assigned to me, all the PRs in the repo, and even the PRs that Copilot has created on my behalf.

Time to select one of the PRs and start our review.

Working with our PR

Opening the PR loads it into the main section of the View Pull Requests tab, but I like to click the “Open in New Tab” option as pops it into a new tab and maximises my screen real estate.

In the view of the PR I have a file browser down the lefthand side, while the main window initially provides me with an overview of the PR, I can read the description, see the comments currently on it, as well as add my own comments.

Clicking on the files within our file list will give me a diff view of the file, and because I’m in Visual Studio we get syntax highlighting of the C#, as well as the list of all the types in the file I’m opening.

When viewing a file that has edits to it rather than a new file, you can choose to view the whole file, or a summary which will condense down the file to hide lines between points that are changed. This can be helpful if you’re viewing a long file and want to avoid excessive scrolling.

We can annotate files in the PR by clicking on the gutter next to the line (or lines if we select multiple first), then opening the inline comment window. Visual Studio will buffer our comments until we submit our review.

Approve and Merge

This PR looks good and is ready to merge into the main branch. In Visual Studio, click Approve in the top-right corner to update its status on GitHub.

The adjacent options let you merge the PR or configure auto-merge while waiting for additional checks. These options follow the policies configured for your repository.

Bringing Copilot in

We might want to get Copilot to act as a pair while we’re reviewing the PR, maybe we want a rubber-ducky review of some of the changes or ask it questions about the solution proposed. To do this, right-click on the PR within the list of active pull requests and select Add to Chat, or from a Copilot session, use #pullrequest:<id> – both of these will add it as context to the session you’re in.

Now you can continue working with Copilot, and it will have the context of that PR available to it as you work.

Wrap-up

Reviewing and actioning pull requests is a daily task for developers, whether they are working on open-source projects, or within their organisation. With Visual Studio, we can perform all of this within the one experience, avoiding the context switching as we jump between tools. This also means that we integration with Visual Studio, such as syntax highlighting and member hierarchy.

items.title: Stop alt-tabbing into the wrong Visual Studio
items.lede: A user asked for per-solution color themes. It already ships, and it goes further than they asked. You run several instances of Visual Studio side by side, one per solution, and they all look identical. Same taskbar icon, same alt-tab thumbnail, same chrome. So, you land in the wrong one, start typing, and realize thirty […]
items.text:
A user asked for per-solution color themes. It already ships, and it goes further than they asked.

You run several instances of Visual Studio side by side, one per solution, and they all look identical. Same taskbar icon, same alt-tab thumbnail, same chrome. So, you land in the wrong one, start typing, and realize thirty seconds later you just edited the wrong repo. Could each solution get its own color theme?

It can. It already does. And the way it works turns out to be more useful than a personal color preference.

How to do it

- Open Tools > Options.

- At the top of the window, find the Applies to dropdown and switch it from your user profile to the current solution.

- Change the color theme.

This uses the new settings experience introduced in Visual Studio 2026.

That’s the whole thing. From that point on, every setting you change applies only to the solution that’s open. Close it, reopen it tomorrow, and the theme comes back with it. Open a different solution and you get its color instead.

No restart, no Apply button, no dialog to dismiss. Most setting changes take effect immediately, and the theme is one of them. The window changes color while you’re still looking at it.

Pick colors with real contrast between the solutions you keep open together. Dark for the service, Blue for the client, Light for the sandbox. The goal is telling them apart from your peripheral vision, not having to read the title bar.

Why this works now

The Applies to dropdown isn’t a color feature. It’s the scoping model behind the new settings experience, and the theme just happens to be the most visible thing you can point at it.

In the old Tools > Options, every page owned its own UI, and settings were a flat, global, machine-wide pile. The new experience puts them all in one consistent, searchable surface backed by JSON, and once settings have a real schema, they can have a real scope. “This value, for this solution” becomes something the IDE can express.

So, the color theme is the demo, not the feature. The feature is that settings now have a scope and a file, and a file is something you can put in source control.

The JSON underneath, and why your team cares

Per-solution settings live in a file called settings.VisualStudio.json, in the solution root folder, right next to your .sln or .slnx. That location is the point.

Commit it, and everyone who clones the repo gets the same setup. A new teammate opens the solution on day one and the IDE already looks and behaves the way the team agreed it should, with no onboarding doc that starts with “first, go to Tools > Options and change these nine things.”

Don’t want to impose your taste on everyone? Add it to .gitignore and it stays yours alone. Same feature, same file. One line decides whether it’s a team convention or a personal preference, and you decide it per repo, after the fact, by whether you commit.

If you’d rather work in the raw values than UI, select Edit user settings as JSON from the toolbar. The file opens showing only what you’ve changed from the defaults, not thousands of lines of untouched values. Edit them there directly or copy a single setting to the clipboard to hand to someone else, which beats screenshotting a checkbox into a Teams chat.

One thing to know

Per-solution settings are stored separately from your user settings, so changing the scope doesn’t overwrite the setup you use everywhere else. Switch the Applies to dropdown back to your user profile whenever you want to change the default for all solutions.

That separation also makes experimentation low risk. Give one solution a distinctive theme, see whether it helps, and remove the solution-level value if it doesn’t. Visual Studio falls back to your user setting without requiring you to reconstruct it.

If you want to go further

Long before this shipped, an extension called Solution Colors solved the same problem from a different angle. It’s color only, and it’s more granular: instead of switching the whole theme, it tints specific parts of the IDE per solution, and it can pick a color automatically, so you don’t have to decide anything.

If per-solution themes are enough, use the built-in feature.

items.title: Today I will… find hidden latency across a distributed .NET application
items.lede: When a distributed application feels slow, the user sees one delay. The code behind that delay may run across a web frontend, backend services, databases, and external APIs. If you profile only the frontend while the backend is slow, the profiler can show that the frontend is healthy without revealing the actual bottleneck. This article […]
items.text:
When a distributed application feels slow, the user sees one delay. The code behind that delay may run across a web frontend, backend services, databases, and external APIs. If you profile only the frontend while the backend is slow, the profiler can show that the frontend is healthy without revealing the actual bottleneck.

This article shows how to narrow a cross-process performance problem with Visual Studio: identify the process that owns the slow operation, capture its CPU activity, inspect the report, and add a focused measurement when CPU samples cannot explain elapsed time. GitHub Copilot Profiler Agent reinforces this workflow with detailed analysis of the captured profile and helps validate the interpretation of the evidence.

The case study uses the Interview Coach sample, a .NET Aspire application with a Blazor frontend and several backend resources. The eventual cause is in an AI streaming path, but the investigation applies to any distributed .NET application where one user action crosses process boundaries.

One symptom, several processes

The Interview Coach Web UI sends a prompt to a backend agent and renders the response as a stream of updates. I tested it with this prompt:

Hi, I'm Peter. Here's my resume: https://justinyoo.github.io/fake-resumes/resume-peter-parker.pdf.
And this is JD: https://justinyoo.github.io/fake-resumes/jd-cloud-solution-architect.pdf

The first complete response took roughly 1.5 to 2 minutes. Some of that time was expected: the first turn parses the PDF into Markdown and stores initial data in Cosmos DB. Even with that work in mind, the response felt slower than expected.

One interaction crossed the Blazor Web UI, the agent, MCP servers, Cosmos DB, and a hosted model. Before looking for a slow method, I needed to establish which process was doing work and which process was waiting.

Visual Studio’s Performance Profiler was a good place to start.

Define the question before collecting data

I reduced the investigation to two questions:

- Which process owned the slow part of the interaction?

- Once that process was isolated, was it computing or waiting?

AppHost starts the Web UI, agent, MCP servers, and data services as separate processes. A profile of InterviewCoach.AppHost describes the orchestrator. It does not automatically describe the Blazor code in InterviewCoach.WebUI.

CPU Usage can collect from multiple processes, which is useful for an initial system-wide view. Here, the visible slowdown occurred while the Web UI consumed and rendered updates, so I wanted a focused capture of that process. I kept the backend resources under Aspire and launched the Web UI as the Visual Studio profiling target.

Target the process that owns the work

This walkthrough assumes the sample is configured for local Azure provisioning and already runs successfully from Visual Studio.

Set InterviewCoach.AppHost as the startup project, select its HTTPS launch profile, and choose Debug > Start Without Debugging. Starting without the debugger leaves AppHost running when the startup project changes later. Once the Aspire resources are ready, stop only the Aspire-managed webui resource from the Aspire dashboard. Leave the agent and its dependencies running.

The standalone Web UI needs a launch profile that uses its own ports and points service discovery at the running agent. In this capture, the agent’s HTTPS endpoint used port 7048. Aspire can assign a different port after a restart, so use the value shown in the dashboard.

Add a Profiler profile under profiles in src/InterviewCoach.WebUI/Properties/launchSettings.json:

"Profiler": {
"commandName": "Project",
"dotnetRunMessages": true,
"launchBrowser": true,
"applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7201;http://localhost:5088",
"environmentVariables": {
"ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development",
"Services__agent__https__0": "localhost:7048"
}
}

The Web UI addresses the agent through a logical service name:

client.BaseAddress = new Uri("https+http://agent");

The environment variable maps to Services:agent:https:0. The configuration-based service discovery provider resolves localhost:7048 as the HTTPS endpoint for agent.

items.title: Today I will… improve test coverage
items.lede: Today I want to look at how we can improve on the test coverage that we have in the Interview Coach application. This application has some unit tests in it already, but I’m sure there is room for improvement. Defining our baseline Before we start writing tests, it’s a good idea to have a baseline […]
items.text:
Today I want to look at how we can improve on the test coverage that we have in the Interview Coach application. This application has some unit tests in it already, but I’m sure there is room for improvement.

Defining our baseline

Before we start writing tests, it’s a good idea to have a baseline of what our coverage is so that we can find out where the gaps are, rather than just writing tests “for the sake of writing tests”.

We can do this using the Analyze Code Coverage for All Tests, from either the Command Palette (CTRL + SHIFT + P) or the Tests menu.

Running the analyzer, we can see where our coverage is sitting:

It looks like our coverage isn’t great, there’s a lot of gaps in the InterviewCoach.Agent project, and then other projects, such as InterviewCoach.Mcp.InterviewData, which doesn’t even have any tests. Let’s start with some tests for the InterviewSessionTool class within that project.

Writing tests with Copilot

The class we’re going to write tests for is a simple class, it takes an interface of our repository, so we can mock the database calls, and the methods receive a payload to work with the repository.

To speed things along, we’re going to use the Test Agent from GitHub Copilot and provide it with the file we want the tests written for.

The agent will analyse the class, then the solution to find the right approach to writing tests. Since we don’t have a test class for the project yet, it’ll generate one, add the references, and then write our test cases.

After a few minutes the agent is done.

It gives a nice summary of what’s been completed, we have 8 new tests added, along with a new test project. The tests were run, and it’s suggesting we run the coverage report again.

This is a considerable improvement on where we were at beforehand.

Full solution test analysis

The Test agent has done a great job at building out the tests for our class, but there’s still a lot of the codebase that doesn’t have tests, and we can use the Test agent to help with that because we can tell it to run across the whole solution and analyze our gaps:

@test #solution

This time, we’re using the #solution context for Copilot, and now the Test agent will analyze all projects and code paths. After a few minutes, Copilot has come back to me with tests covering the repository, the DbContext, our extension methods, as well as more tests in the InterviewCoach.Agent project. It also identified that there was no value in writing tests for files such as AgentMode.cs since it just contains an enum, thus there’s nothing to test.

With this, our coverage is up to 81%, up from 37% to start with, and includes three projects we originally didn’t have tests for at all.

Wrap-up

While we know the value of writing tests, knowing where we should invest that effort is something that is often overlooked. Using the Code Coverage analysis in Visual Studio gives us that overview, so we can identify the gaps in our testing, then combining that with the Test agent, we can build out targeted tests for a single class or perform a solution-wide analysis and uplift.

items.title: AI is changing how we code. It’s also changing how we learn.
items.lede: AI is changing software development at a pace no one can ignore. Developers now have powerful AI tools that can help us write code, understand unfamiliar codebases, troubleshoot problems, learn new frameworks, and get answers in seconds. That is an incredible opportunity.
items.text:
AI is changing software development at a pace no one can ignore.

Developers now have powerful AI tools that can help us write code, understand unfamiliar codebases, troubleshoot problems, learn new frameworks, and get answers in seconds. That is an incredible opportunity. But as these tools become more capable, I believe something else is becoming more valuable too: learning directly from other developers.

That’s one of the reasons I continue to believe so strongly in events like VSLive!.

Learn from people who have done the work

One of the things I value most about VSLive! is its focus on practical developer education.

For more than three decades, VSLive! has helped developers, software architects, and engineers stay current as Microsoft development has evolved. Today, that means learning about AI-powered development alongside the technologies developers are already using to build applications.

You’re learning from experts who can explain not only how something works, but why they chose one approach over another and what they learned along the way.

That context is difficult to reproduce outside of this kind of event.

Get hands-on and ask the next question

VSLive! gives developers opportunities to move beyond simply hearing about a technology. When you encounter an unexpected error, question a design choice, or discover that your implementation behaves differently than expected, you can dig deeper.

And because you’re learning alongside experts and other developers, you can ask the next question.

That feedback loop can turn an interesting technology into something you’re confident enough to bring back to your team.

The hallway can be as valuable as the session

Some of the most useful moments at a developer conference don’t happen on a slide.

They happen after a session when you ask the speaker one more question. They happen over lunch when another developer explains how their team solved a problem you’ve been wrestling with. Sometimes they happen because you meet someone who becomes part of your professional network for years.

VSLive! creates room for those conversations alongside the technical content and access to Microsoft Product Managers.

Step away from the backlog and think about what comes next

Most developers don’t spend their normal workday thinking broadly about where software development is headed. They’re fixing bugs, reviewing pull requests, shipping features, attending meetings, and working through the backlog.

A conference gives you an opportunity to step outside that cycle and ask bigger questions:

What should I learn next?

How should AI change the way I build software?

What are other teams doing with .NET, Azure, GitHub Copilot, and modern application architecture?

What could I bring back that would make my team better?

VSLive! gives you a place to explore those questions with people who are asking many of the same things.

Put your Visual Studio subscriber benefit to work

If you’re trying to keep pace with AI while deepening your skills in .NET, C#, Azure, modern software engineering, data, web development, and the Microsoft developer stack, there is real value in spending a few days learning alongside other developers in expert led sessions.

items.title: Visual Studio September Update – Power Your Workflow with Your Model
items.lede: Bring your own AI model with updates to BYOM, fix NuGet vulnerabilities from the Error List, explore pull requests with the Git agent, see which operand decides an if condition, and attach to Podman containers.
items.text:
The best LLM in Visual Studio is the one you choose. This month’s update puts that idea front and center: pick the model that fits how you work, then use it everywhere GitHub Copilot already helps you today, from fixing vulnerable packages to reviewing pull requests. And once you’re in the editor, you’ll find sharper debugging tools too, whichever model is doing the thinking alongside you.

Grab the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel update and let us know what’s working and where we should invest next.

Updates to Bring Your Own Model

The best AI in Visual Studio is the AI you can bring with you. With Bring Your Own Model (BYOM), more developers can use AI in Visual Studio with the models their teams prefer, whether through GitHub Copilot or their own model deployments. From individual developers experimenting with new models to organizations standardizing on approved deployments, BYOM lets you use AI your way, whether or not you’re signed in to GitHub.

https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/vs18.10_BYOMShortVideo.mp4

BYOM is available in preview and enabled by default across the Community, Professional, and Enterprise SKUs. Connect to a Microsoft Foundry deployment or another supported provider, including custom endpoints for OpenAI and Ollama, then work in Agent Mode with the new Agent (Preview).

This is an early preview, and we want your feedback. Not every model supports every Agent Mode capability yet. When a feature isn’t supported, Visual Studio marks it clearly instead of failing silently. Try it and tell us what’s working and where we should invest next in the Developer Community forum or fill out this short survey.

To get started: open Chat, open the model picker and choose Add a model or Manage Models, connect to your provider, then start working in Agent Mode. Supported providers are Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama, with custom endpoint support for OpenAI and Ollama.

This release has breaking changes for the BYOM capability: BYOM now works with the new Agent (Preview), which is built on the GitHub Copilot SDK-powered harness. The earlier BYOM experience in the previous Ask and Agent modes is no longer supported; install the latest Visual Studio release and use the new Agent (Preview) to try it. Previously added Ollama models will need to be re-added after this update due to a few backend updates for that provider.

Fix NuGet Vulnerabilities from the Error List

Whichever model you’ve chosen, it can now help you close security gaps the moment they surface. NuGet Audit warnings in the Visual Studio Error List give you a direct way to fix vulnerable packages with GitHub Copilot instead of tracking them down manually.

After a restore reports an NU1901, NU1902, NU1903, or NU1904 warning, select the sparkle action in the Fixer column. This opens GitHub Copilot Chat in agent mode and asks Copilot to fix the vulnerable NuGet packages using the NuGet MCP server.

To use the fix: restore a solution that contains a package with a known vulnerability, open View > Error List and find the NuGet Audit warning, select the sparkle action in the Fixer column, then review and apply the changes Copilot proposes. You’ll need to be signed in to GitHub Copilot, and automated fixes also require the NuGet MCP server, which is built into Visual Studio and can be enabled from the Copilot Chat tools menu.

Explore Pull Requests with the Git Agent

Reviewing a pull request usually means piecing together the discussion thread, the changed files, and what actually matters before you can dig in. The Git agent can now do that legwork for you, powered by whichever model you’ve connected.

Open GitHub Copilot Chat, select the Git agent, and ask it about your pull request, attaching the pull request as context from the Git Repository window. The response includes navigable links that open the corresponding comments and files directly in the pull request view in the IDE, so you can jump straight to what matters instead of scrolling to find it. Ask follow-up questions any time you want the agent to go deeper.

items.title: New tools, new workflows and the value of the Visual Studio Subscription: What we learned at VSLive! San Diego
items.lede: What happens when developers who have spent decades working with Visual Studio start rethinking how they write code, learn new skills, and expand their access to development tools? At VSLive! San Diego, we had an opportunity to find out as developers gathered for five days of technical sessions, hands-on learning, and conversations about Visual Studio, […]
items.text:
What happens when developers who have spent decades working with Visual Studio start rethinking how they write code, learn new skills, and expand their access to development tools?

At VSLive! San Diego, we had an opportunity to find out as developers gathered for five days of technical sessions, hands-on learning, and conversations about Visual Studio, .NET, AI, cloud, data, and modern application development.

One of the most interesting things we heard in San Diego was how readily experienced developers are adopting new tools and workflows.

GitHub Copilot is part of that story, and developers aren’t limiting themselves to a single AI experience. They’re building broader, more differentiated tool kits. But they aren’t necessarily replacing familiar tools. They’re expanding how they work, choosing different experiences depending on the task, and finding new ways to solve problems.

This is why events like VSLive! provide such an amazing opportunity for developers tackling these kinds of changes. Not only do they get to learn from expert led sessions and hands on labs, they get to learn from each other.

AI is changing how developers approach unfamiliar problems

One of the best parts of this event was being able to explore how developers learn new technologies and work through challenges.

AI is increasingly becoming an early step in that process.

Developers are using AI to research unfamiliar topics, understand existing code, troubleshoot problems, and explore possible approaches before deciding what to try next.

But they aren’t relying on AI alone.

They still move between documentation, technical videos, sample code, and hands-on experimentation to develop a deeper understanding of what they’re building. And a significant number of participants shared that hands-on learning was a preferred way to learn.

That stood out to me.

Even as developers adopt AI-assisted workflows, they continue to value opportunities to work directly with technology, test ideas, and understand how things behave. AI may help developers get started faster. Experimentation helps them decide what to do with what they’ve learned.

The suite of benefits offered through a Visual Studio Subscription complements this developer journey, not only by providing significant discounts at VSLive! events, but also through access to learning paths, Azure credits, certifications, and hands-on labs.

More generated code means more to evaluate

Another interesting observation was how AI is changing the work that happens after code is written. Developers told us AI helps them produce code faster, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re spending less time on development.

Instead, they’re spending more time reviewing and validating generated code. Does it work as expected? Does it fit the architecture? Is it secure? Can someone maintain it later?

These questions have always mattered. AI-assisted development makes them even more important as developers evaluate code they may not have written themselves.

AI can accelerate development, but developer resourcing and judgment remains essential.

Time is still the biggest obstacle to learning

With so many learning resources available, you might expect developers to struggle with finding the right information. But our conversations with developers at VSLive! San Diego signaled that the biggest barriers to learning new skills are time and the pace of technological change.

Sometimes developers need a quick explanation to move forward. Other times, they need a course, a technical session, a community, or an environment where they can experiment.

That helps explain why the flexible learning environment at VSlive! matters now more than ever. And it’s another reason Visual Studio Subscription benefits remain valuable. They aren’t just about the software developers use today. They can also help support the technologies and skills developers want to explore next.

Let’s keep the conversation going

What stood out most from San Diego was the combination of experience and curiosity. We met developers who have used Visual Studio for decades and are actively exploring how AI can change the way they build software.

items.title: Stop waiting on a failed build
items.lede: Stop solution builds after the first project failure so you can return to fixing the error sooner.
items.text:
A project fails to compile, but the solution build keeps going. You already have an error to fix, while other projects continue using build time to tell you the solution still doesn’t build.

Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11 adds an opt-in way to stop a solution build after the first project failure. If your next step is to fix that failure and try again, you can make the build stop there too.

Choose when the build should stop

Open Tools > Options > Projects and Solutions > Build and Run and enable Stop solution build after first failure.

When a project fails, Visual Studio stops starting queued projects and safely stops projects already building. It still reports the build as failed, not canceled. You don’t have to watch for the first error and manually cancel the remaining work.

This stops the solution build, not only the projects that depend on the failed project. That’s an important choice: you get back to the first problem sooner, but you don’t collect the results of every remaining project in that build.

If you prefer to see those results before you start fixing errors, leave the setting disabled. That preserves the existing behavior. You can also turn it off again on the same settings page.

Measure the wait after a failure

In four test builds, post-failure completion time averaged 26 seconds with the setting disabled and 1.5 seconds with it enabled. That’s about a 94% reduction in the wait after a failure, not a claim that successful builds run 94% faster.

Your results depend on the solution and where a failure occurs. A solution with a long dependency chain or substantial parallel work can have more remaining work to stop than a small solution that finishes almost immediately anyway.

The Developer Community request describes a concrete version of this problem: a packaging project kept trying to build even after a dependency failed. The new option gives you a solution-wide stopping policy rather than requiring you to interrupt the build yourself.

Keep the two decisions separate

This setting answers when should a failed build stop? It doesn’t decide which projects you build in the first place. Existing Build and Run options cover choices such as building only startup projects and dependencies when you run or debug.

Try stop-on-failure on a solution where you normally cancel the build after seeing an error. Compare that post-failure wait, then keep the policy that fits how you troubleshoot.

items.title: Organize and revisit tabs with the keyboard
items.lede: Reorder your document tabs and return to them by visual position with new keyboard shortcuts.
items.text:
When you’re moving between an implementation, its tests, and a related interface, the order of your open tabs can become a useful part of the task. But arranging that order and returning to a particular position shouldn’t require a mouse trip each time.

Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11 adds keyboard commands for both jobs: move the active tab into position, then jump directly to a tab by its visual position. The connection is the tab order itself. You can arrange a small working set and navigate that arrangement from the keyboard.

Put the active tab where you want it

Use Ctrl + Shift + PgUp to move the active tab one position left, or Ctrl + Shift + PgDn to move it one position right.

For example, move a test file next to its implementation before you start comparing them. The command moves the tab; it doesn’t switch to the neighboring document.

If you use vertical tabs, the same shortcuts move the active tab up or down. They also work for tool windows hosted in the document well.

The commands respect the organization you’ve already chosen:

- Pinned tabs stay in the pinned section, and unpinned tabs stay in theirs.

- A vertical tab stays within its project group.

- Alphabetical sorting prevents manual reordering.

- Preview tabs can’t be moved.

The request for keyboard tab movement makes a useful distinction between moving and switching. One commenter described pinning and unpinning tabs as a workaround for arranging them without the mouse. These commands address arrangement directly.

Return to a position directly

Use Ctrl + NumPad1 through Ctrl + NumPad9 to activate the corresponding visible document tab in the active document group.

The mapping follows visual order, including pinned and unpinned tabs. Preview tabs don’t consume a slot. If you switch document groups, the shortcuts use the order in the newly active group.

That makes these position shortcuts, not permanent assignments to filenames. Reordering a tab changes which document occupies that position. Arrange the files first, then use their positions while you work.

Give tool window tabs the space they need

Tab layout matters for tool windows, too. If you dock Error List and Package Manager Console in the same group, the shorter label no longer needs a tab as wide as the longer one. Tool window tabs now size individually rather than all taking the width of the longest label.

The request for individually sized tool window tabs describes that wasted space directly. You can also set minimum and maximum tool window tab widths independently of document tabs in Tools > Options > All Settings > Environment > Tabs > Tool Window Tabs.

Document tabs, tool window tabs, and window headers now share a consistent 24-pixel height. When you arrange tabs with the mouse, the drop preview aligns more accurately with their destination. High-contrast fixes also keep tab borders from being clipped.

Keep your preferred bindings

You can find Window.MoveTabLeft and Window.MoveTabRight in Tools > Options > Environment > Keyboard and assign other shortcuts. The numbered-tab commands also participate in keyboard customization.

The new movement defaults replace the Text Editor bindings for Edit.ViewTopExtend and Edit.ViewBottomExtend. Those commands still exist, so reassign them if they’re part of your editing routine.

For background on pinned tabs, preview tabs, and document groups, see Customize window layouts and personalize tabs. Those existing layout choices still determine the structure these commands work within.

Start with two or three documents from your current task. Put them in a useful order, then try returning to them by position instead of cycling through every open tab.

items.title: Compare today’s code with an earlier commit
items.lede: Compare a historical commit with your working tree without checking out the commit or leaving your branch.
items.text:
You know a change was present in an earlier commit, and you want to see how the code in front of you differs now. Comparing two commits answers part of that question, but it leaves out work you haven’t committed yet.

Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11 adds Compare with Working Tree to the repository-level commit workflow. You can compare a historical commit with your current code without checking out that commit or leaving your current branch.

- Open commit history or use the branch list to reach the commit you want to inspect.

- Right-click the commit and select Compare with Working Tree.

- In the compare view, select changed files to inspect their diffs.

items.title: Keep your investigation between sessions
items.lede: Start a standalone Markdown note and use the opt-in Hot Exit preview to resume unsaved work next session.
items.text:
A bug investigation often starts with a few notes: what you tried, which input reproduced the problem, and what you want to check next. You might not be ready to choose a filename or add those notes to a project. You still want them there when you return.

In Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11, you can create a standalone Markdown file from New File and use the opt-in Hot Exit preview feature to resume that unfinished note after closing and reopening Visual Studio. Start the note while the details are fresh, then return to it next session.

Start the note without adding a project item

- Press Ctrl + N to open New File.

- Select Markdown File.

- Select Open and start writing.

This is separate from Add New Item, which creates a project item. The original feedback specifically asked for a Markdown template in New File, including when working without an open solution.

The Markdown editor itself isn’t new in this release. You can use it to turn your notes into headings, lists, and fenced code blocks, then check the rendered result. The Markdown preview guide explains its editing and preview controls.

Resume the same unfinished note

Hot Exit is off by default. To enable it, go to Tools > Options, expanding All Settings > Projects and Solutions > General, and selecting Reopen unsaved documents on solution load or empty environment.

With Hot Exit enabled, closing Visual Studio preserves session state. When you reopen Visual Studio, it restores open documents and unsaved edits, including new files you haven’t saved yet. Your note can remain unfinished without forcing you to choose a permanent home for it before you close the IDE.

Hot Exit also preserves changes to previously saved files, your tab and window layout, and undo functionality for saved files. For those saved files, you can continue using Ctrl + Z after restoring the session.

This is session preservation, not the same thing as deliberately saving a document to disk or committing it to source control. Save the note when you want to share it or keep it as part of the repository. The useful choice here is that a temporary note doesn’t have to become a project artifact merely to survive a normal close and reopen.

The Hot Exit request calls out exploratory work and temporary files as reasons to preserve unsaved documents. Keep the preview option off if you prefer your current close-and-save workflow.

Try the combination with a disposable investigation note: write down the next thing to check, close Visual Studio with Hot Exit enabled, and reopen it to continue the note.

items.title: Visual Studio October Update – Compare Commits to Your Code, Resolve Conflicts in Bulk, Keep Coding
items.lede: Compare commits with your working tree, resolve merge conflicts in bulk, and keep coding with refreshed Copilot chat, Hot Exit, keyboard tab controls, and Fonts and Colors.
items.text:
The October Visual Studio update gives you a clearer view of how your code has changed and more control over resolving merge conflicts. Compare an earlier commit directly with your current working tree, including edits still in progress, and apply the same conflict resolution across multiple files at once.

There’s more to try beyond Git: a new Copilot chat experience, Hot Exit for unfinished work, keyboard shortcuts for organizing tabs, and a refreshed Fonts and Colors page. Update to the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel to get started.

Compare a Commit to Your Working Tree

Need to see how your current code differs from an earlier commit? You can now compare that commit directly with your working tree across your repository, including committed changes and edits still in progress. Use it to review a refactor across several commits or investigate what’s changed since a known-good version.

From commit history or the branch list in the Git Repository window, right-click a commit and select Compare with Working Tree. The compare view lets you browse changed files and inspect their diffs against the code you have today.

Bulk Resolve Merge Conflicts

When you already know which side to keep across several conflicted files, you shouldn’t have to repeat that choice for every file. You can now resolve conflicts across a group of files at once.

In Git Changes, right-click multiple selected files, a folder, or the repository root under Unmerged Changes and select Keep All Current or Take All Incoming. The selected resolution applies to all selected files, or all conflicted files within the selected folder or repository.

Try the New Copilot Chat Experience

The new GitHub Copilot Chat experience builds on the Copilot SDK foundation introduced with Agent (Preview). That foundation now extends to Ask mode, Agent mode, and the underlying chat infrastructure, sharing the SDK used by the Copilot CLI and GitHub Copilot app.

It brings more capable end-to-end agent workflows with less back-and-forth, longer-running sessions with more effective prompt caching, and consistent behavior across Copilot experiences. To try it, open Tools > Options > GitHub > Copilot > Copilot Chat, select Use new Copilot chat experience, then restart Visual Studio.

Enable it for your next coding session and let us know how it handles the work. If something is missing or isn’t working, use Help > Send Feedback > Report a Problem to tell us.

Keep Unsaved Work with Hot Exit

Closing Visual Studio doesn’t have to mean deciding where to save every unfinished file. Hot Exit preserves your unsaved work between sessions, including new files you haven’t saved and edits to existing files.

When you reopen Visual Studio, it restores those documents and changes, along with your tab and window layout. It also preserves undo functionality for saved files, including Ctrl+Z. Hot Exit is off by default; to enable it, open Tools > Options, expand All Settings > Projects and Solutions > General, and select Reopen unsaved documents on solution load or empty environment.

https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/10/vs18.11_HotExit.mp4

Move Documents with the Keyboard

You can now reorder tabs without reaching for the mouse. Press Ctrl+Shift+PgUp to move the active tab left or Ctrl+Shift+PgDn to move it right. With vertical tabs, the same shortcuts move it up or down. They work for documents and tool windows hosted in the document well.

Pinned and unpinned tabs stay separate. Vertical tabs stay within their project group, and manual reordering isn’t available when alphabetical sorting is enabled. Preview tabs can’t be moved.

You can remap Window.MoveTabLeft and Window.MoveTabRight in Tools > Options > Environment > Keyboard. The defaults replace the previous Text Editor bindings for Edit.ViewTopExtend and Edit.ViewBottomExtend; those commands remain available if you want to assign them different shortcuts.

Personalize Fonts and Colors

Finding the right editor customization is easier with the refreshed Fonts and Colors experience, now built on Unified Settings.

Let’s look at a few ways you can put those benefits to work.

Interested in AI-powered applications?

If Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Apps and Agents Developer is a certification you’re considering, your subscriber benefits can provide a useful starting point preparing for the required AI-103 exam.

items.title: Copilot in Visual Studio Just Got a Major Upgrade
items.lede: Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, […]
items.text:
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, new ways to work.

We put the previous and new Copilot experiences through over one hundred coding tasks. The new experience came out ahead with every model we tested, across capability levels and providers, resolving up to 21 more tasks.

The chat itself is better too: you get shorter, more focused answers, you can steer Copilot mid-task and see what each request costs.

More Tasks Solved

To measure what matters to .NET developers, the .NET team built a benchmark from real issues in real C# projects, across .NET Framework and .NET Core, Azure and Aspire, and WinForms and desktop apps. We ran both Copilot chat experiences through 157 of its tasks. A task counts as resolved only when its failing tests pass without breaking any that already passed.

The new engine has also been tested on C++, Python, and a range of other languages.

One example from our own backlog: a user reported that long answer choices in Copilot’s questions were getting cut off. We asked Copilot to help reproduce it, once in the previous experience and once in the new SDK-powered experience. The previous experience came back with steps for us to reproduce it by hand. The new one did something we didn’t expect: it realized it was running inside the very chat window that had the bug, so it reproduced the problem right there.

Same Models, Better Harness

On its own, a model reads text and writes text. It can’t open your solution, edit a file, or run your tests. The harness is everything around the model that turns text into real work: what the model sees, which tools it can use, what it remembers, and what it’s allowed to touch. Give the same model a better harness, and you get better results.

Through the SDK, Copilot in Visual Studio now runs on the Microsoft Copilot harness. It’s battle-tested at the scale of millions of users, and GitHub designed it to be fast and predictable. Here’s what you’ll notice:

- It finishes the job. The harness keeps Copilot going until the task is actually done.

- It gets to the point. One developer described the experience as “Less chatter, more quality results for large tasks”.

New in Copilot Chat

The new engine also changes how you work with Copilot. Here’s what you won’t find in the previous experience.

- Steer it while it works. No more waiting for Copilot to finish before you change course. Type a new instruction and press Enter, and Copilot picks it up mid-task. Until it does, your message is marked Pending, and you can select the X to take it back.

- See what Copilot actually did. Every step shows what came back, not just what Copilot tried. Expand a step to see the results, open them in the editor, or copy the exact command Copilot ran.

- Watch subagents at work. When Copilot hands off part of a task to a subagent, the subagent gets its own card showing which model it’s using and every step it takes, live.

- Work beyond your solution. Point Copilot at any folder on your machine from the chat header or attach whole folders as context.

- Get a second opinion. With Agent selected, type / to call on one of the built-in agents. /security-review runs a security-focused review of your changes to find vulnerabilities, and /rubber-duck has a different model critique Copilot’s plan before it acts.

Still Unmistakably Visual Studio

Because it’s the same technology, Copilot behaves more consistently across Visual Studio, VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Write an agent skill once, and it works in all four without modifications. Improve the harness, and every surface benefits.

But the same engine doesn’t mean a one-size-fits-all experience. Copilot still works with the tools you rely on in Visual Studio. Specialized agents help you debug, profile, fix build failures, modernize .NET apps, and speed up C++ builds.

items.title: Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11
items.lede: Today, we are announcing Visual Studio 2026 Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 18.11 alongside Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on the Stable channel. LTSC 18.11 will receive two years of support, through November 14, 2028, rather than the one year of LTSC support we previously announced. items.text:
Today, we are announcing Visual Studio 2026 Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 18.11 alongside Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on the Stable channel. LTSC 18.11 will receive two years of support, through November 14, 2028, rather than the one year of LTSC support we previously announced. If you are using Visual Studio 2022 for its LTSC benefits this is a great time to consider migrating to the new Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 to get the latest Visual Studio has to offer.

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 is not a new product – it is a new support and servicing channel for Visual Studio 2026 so it includes the full feature set, capabilities, and fixes as Visual Studio 2026 18.0 through 18.10. If you have stayed on Visual Studio 2022 while waiting for a Visual Studio 2026 LTSC release with LTS toolsets, you should begin planning validation and deployment of LTSC 18.11.

View the Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 Release Notes

We are not changing how the Stable channel works. Stable will continue receiving monthly feature and quality updates. If you are on Stable and want to keep receiving those updates, you do not need to change anything. LTSC is an option if your organization needs to stay on a fixed release.

Why are we making this change?

In November 2025, we announced a new release and support model with Visual Studio 2026, including one year on Stable followed by one year of LTSC support. Customers told us that one year of LTSC support did not leave enough time to validate and deploy a release. The longer support period gives those organizations more time to deploy and use LTSC 18.11.

An LTSC release with LTS toolsets

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 will include Long-Term Support (LTS) toolsets for .NET and C++ development: .NET 10 LTS and MSVC 14.50 and 14.52. The MSVC and .NET toolsets in Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 will be supported per their respective support lifecycles, which are at least as long as the support lifecycle for Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11.

Stable is for feature updates and servicing, we recommend this as the default

Stable remains the recommended channel if you want the latest Visual Studio features, including new GitHub Copilot capabilities. To remain supported on Stable, keep your installation current with its monthly updates. Stable is where most customers will be and we strongly recommend this channel so you can receive and take advantage of the latest features Visual Studio has to offer.

LTSC will get servicing only

LTSC 18.11 will receive security and other critical fixes, we do not plan to ship regular feature updates for LTSC like we will for the Stable cannel. If you choose LTSC to limit feature changes in your development environment, you still need to keep your installation current with LTSC servicing updates to remain supported.

Existing Visual Studio 2026 keys continue to work

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 is not a new product, the product remains Visual Studio 2026. Today’s announcement is a new channel for the existing product. Therefore, existing Visual Studio 2026 product keys will continue to work on both Stable and LTSC 18.11 for Enterprise, Professional, and the Build Tools SKUs. You do not need a new key or another purchase of Visual Studio 2026 to use either channel.

Getting started

If your organization has stayed on Visual Studio 2022 while waiting for a Visual Studio 2026 LTSC release with LTS toolsets, you should begin planning validation and deployment of LTSC 18.11.

Before deployment, review Visual Studio Product Lifecycle and Servicing for support requirements and installation and deployment guidance. Refer to this guidance for information about Switching between Stable and LTSC channels. You can find more details about this release in the Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 release notes.

items.title: Bring Your Own Model is now generally available in Visual Studio
items.lede: Whether your team hosts its own AI models, you have an API key from a model provider, or you want to experiment with a model running on your machine, Bring Your Own Model (BYOM) lets you use those models without leaving Visual Studio. BYOM is now generally available in Visual Studio 18.12. Since the August […]
items.text:
Whether your team hosts its own AI models, you have an API key from a model provider, or you want to experiment with a model running on your machine, Bring Your Own Model (BYOM) lets you use those models without leaving Visual Studio.

BYOM is now generally available in Visual Studio 18.12. Since the August Preview, your feedback has shaped improvements for team deployments, enterprise networks, and personal projects. This release brings multiple configurations for the same provider, a dedicated custom-endpoint experience that includes local models, more control over API compatibility, and improved proxy support.

No GitHub sign-in is required. If you can’t access GitHub, you can still use your chosen models in Visual Studio—including local or internally hosted models in air-gapped environments—provided the model endpoint is reachable and its authentication requirements are met.

More than one connection to the same provider

Your work doesn’t always fit into a single provider configuration. You might use one account for personal projects and another for work, connect to separate Microsoft Foundry resources, or keep an experimental deployment alongside your team’s approved endpoint.

You can now keep multiple configurations for the same provider and give them meaningful names, such as “Work” and “Personal.” Each keeps its own connection details and models, so you can choose the right setup without removing and re-adding a provider.

https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/11/Two-Endpoints-Cropped.mp4

A clearer path to custom endpoints

Many developers don’t connect directly to a model vendor’s public endpoint. You might use a self-hosted inference server, an AI gateway, or an endpoint provided by your organization.

The new Custom Endpoint provider gives OpenAI-compatible services, including OpenRouter, their own place in provider configuration. Enter your endpoint URL and an API key if required. Where the endpoint provides a compatible model listing, Visual Studio can surface the models it returns.

You can also connect to local models served by LM Studio. Start the local server, then add its OpenAI-compatible URL using Custom Endpoint to use your model in Visual Studio’s Agent Mode.

Match the API to your model

When adding a custom model, you can now select the API format supported by your provider: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Responses, or Anthropic-compatible Messages. You can also view and change the configured format in Manage models

You can also configure context size, maximum output, tool calling, and vision support to match your model and deployment.

Better suited to enterprise environments

For organizations, model choice needs to work with existing network settings and policies.

We’ve improved proxy support so provider connections and Agent Mode both use Visual Studio’s resolved proxy configuration.

Administrators can enable or disable BYOM through organizational policy.

Getting Started

Try BYOM in Visual Studio:

- Install Visual Studio 18.12 GA.

- Open Chat and use the model picker to choose Manage models.

- Choose Add model provider, then select Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, or Custom Endpoint.

- Configure the connection, give it a meaningful name, and add the models you want to use.

- Select your model and start working in Agent Mode.

Note: If you don’t see Add model provider, your organization’s administrator may have disabled bring-your-own-model access.

Keep shaping what comes next

We’re continuing to learn from the models, deployments, and environments you use. Tell us what’s working, where setup still gets in your way, and what would make BYOM more useful through the Developer Community forum or our short survey.

Your feedback is helping shape what comes next. Happy coding!
